Hands-On Activity

This activity is designed to move you from theory to practice. You'll use NotebookLM to analyze Ford Motor Company, transforming a collection of documents into a dynamic and queryable knowledge base.

Objective: To learn the core workflow of NotebookLM by exploring single sources, synthesizing information across multiple sources, and generating structured summaries.

docs.title: Gather Your Sources
docs.text:
Download source documents here

To begin, download the curated set of files I have put together for you. This collection includes Ford's latest Form 10-K, proxy filings, and a Q4 earnings call transcript. You'll also find a text file containing links to a YouTube interview and a Google Doc. This variety is intentional—it highlights NotebookLM's ability to handle diverse source formats, including PDFs, TXT files, and even content from Google Drive and YouTube links.

docs.title: Create Your Notebook & Explore the Interface
docs.text:
Now, let's set up your workspace.

  1. Navigate to NotebookLM and create a new notebook named "Ford Company Analysis."
  2. Upload all the files from Step 1 into your new notebook.
  3. Take a moment to get familiar with the interface, which is organized into three main panels:
    • Sources Panel (Left): This is your library. All the documents you've uploaded are listed here. You can click on any source to view it.
    • Chat Panel (Center): This is your main interaction space. Here, you'll ask questions and receive AI-generated, source-grounded answers.
    • Studio (Right): This is your project workspace. Think of it as a smart notebook where you can save key insights from the chat, write your own notes, and generate high-level summaries of your sources.

docs.title: Dive into a Single Source
docs.text:
Before asking questions across all documents, let's explore just one.

  1. In the Sources panel, click on the Form 10-K document.
  2. The document will open, and alongside it, NotebookLM will automatically generate a Source Guide. This guide includes a summary, key topics, and even suggested questions.
  3. Click on one of the Key Topics (e.g., "Risk Factors" or "Business Segments").
  4. Observe how clicking the topic automatically populates the Chat panel with a question and generates a detailed, cited answer. This is a powerful way to get a quick overview of a long document.

docs.title: Ask Questions Across ALL Sources
docs.text:
The true power of NotebookLM is its ability to synthesize information from all your sources at once. Use the chat feature to ask broader questions that require connecting ideas from different documents.

Try these prompts:

Based on all sources, what are the biggest contradictions you can find between the risks listed in the 10-K and the optimistic tone of the earnings call?

Synthesize the leadership's main strategic priorities as mentioned in the earnings call, the 10-K, and the CEO's YouTube interview.

Create a list of all the members of the Board of Directors and note any concerns raised about them in the proxy statement.

docs.title: Synthesize and Summarize
docs.text:
The Studio is where you bring everything together. It helps you create powerful summaries that collate information from all your documents.

  1. At the top of the Studio, you will see suggestions for generating audio and video overviews, mind map and reports like an FAQ, a Briefing Doc, or a Study Guide. Click one to create a comprehensive, AI-generated summary of your sources.
  2. You can also create custom summaries. For example, You can choose language, length, what topics and sources AI hosts should focus on via customize option.
  3. Once the overview is generated, you can access it in the Studio. This allows you to build a custom dashboard of insights, combining automatically generated summaries with your own specific queries.

docs.title: Conclusion: Your Project Workspace
docs.text: As you've seen, working in NotebookLM is fundamentally different from a one-off chat with Gemini. NotebookLM is a project workspace centered around a specific set of source documents. The Chat feature is your tool for ad-hoc querying and exploring specific lines of inquiry. The Studio is where you synthesize your findings, saving key answers and generating powerful overviews that bring together all the information from your source documents.

docs.title: Writing Good Prompts
docs.text:
The Art of the Prompt: How to Talk to an AI

We've all been trained by years of using search engines to communicate in short, keyword-driven phrases like "Ford stock price" or "EV market risks." This works for search engines because their job is to find and rank existing web pages.

AI assistants, however, work differently. Their job is to generate new text based on the instructions you provide. Giving an AI a search-style query is like walking up to a brilliant but very literal assistant and just saying "market risks." You might get an answer, but it won't be tailored, specific, or particularly insightful.

To get a truly valuable response, you need to shift from searching to instructing. You need to provide the same kind of detail you would give a human collaborator. The good news is that there's a simple, robust framework for doing this.

docs.title: The Four Pillars of a Robust Prompt
docs.text:
Think of every great prompt as having four pillars that support it. You might not use every single one every time, but knowing them will help you craft much more effective requests.

  1. 👤 Role: Tell the AI who to be. Assigning a role is the fastest way to change the tone, style, and perspective of the response.

    • Example: "Act as a skeptical investor," or "Explain this to me like I'm a 15-year-old," or "You are a marketing executive..."

  2. 📝 Task: State precisely what you want the AI to do. Use clear, specific action verbs instead of vague questions.

    • Example: Instead of "What about the risks?", try "Summarize the top 3 risks..." or "Compare and contrast the risks mentioned in these two documents..."

  3. CONTEXT: Provide the necessary background information. This is where you ground the AI in the same reality you're in, preventing generic answers.

    • Example: "...based on the attached 10-K report," or "Given that our primary marketing goal is to reach a new demographic..."

  4. FORMAT: Specify exactly how you want the output presented. This saves you time and makes the response immediately useful.

    • Example: "...in a bulleted list," or "...as a three-paragraph email draft," or "...in a table with two columns."

docs.title: Putting It All Together: A Before-and-After Example
docs.text: Let's see how this framework transforms a vague query into a powerful instruction.

docs.title: The "Search Engine" Prompt (Before)
docs.text:
Imagine you want to understand the challenges Ford is facing. You might type:

Ford risks

Likely Outcome: You'll get a generic, Wikipedia-style paragraph listing common business risks like "economic downturns," "competition," and "market shifts." It's true, but it's not insightful or specific to the company's current situation. It's not actionable.

docs.title: The "Robust" Prompt (After)
docs.text:
Now, let's build a prompt using the four pillars:

[👤 Role] "Act as a financial analyst for a major investment firm. [📝 Task] Your task is to summarize the top 3 strategic risks for your client. [CONTEXT] Use only the information found in Ford's most recent annual 10-K report. Focus specifically on risks related to their transition to electric vehicles. [FORMAT] Please present your summary as a bulleted list. For each risk, provide a one-sentence explanation of its potential impact on the company's profitability."

Likely Outcome: You will receive a targeted, specific, and professionally-toned summary that looks something like this:

  • Supply Chain Disruptions for EV Components: A failure to secure a stable supply of batteries and semiconductors could delay production targets, directly impacting revenue and market share.
  • Intensifying Competition in the EV Market: The influx of new and established competitors could lead to price wars and higher marketing costs, potentially squeezing profit margins.
  • Uncertainty in Consumer Adoption Rates: A slower-than-expected adoption of EVs by the mass market could result in underutilized factory capacity and losses on capital investments.

This second response is infinitely more valuable. It's tailored, contextual, and formatted for immediate use. By taking 30 seconds to design your prompt, you save yourself from wading through generic information and get directly to the insight you need.

docs.title: Pro-Tips for Better Prompts
docs.text: Beyond the four pillars, here are a few extra techniques you can use to level up your AI collaboration.

docs.title: 1. Provide an Example of What You Want 🎨
docs.text:
If you need the AI to follow a very specific style or format, the easiest way to get it right is to show it exactly what you mean. This is far more effective than trying to describe the format with words.

  • Instead of describing: "Please summarize the key points of the article in a very concise, journalistic style."
  • Try showing an example: "Summarize the key points of the attached article. Follow this example format:
    • Headline: A short, catchy title (e.g., 'Ford Pivots to EV Dominance')
    • Key takeaway: A single sentence summary (e.g., 'Ford's latest strategy bets heavily on electrifying its most popular truck lines to capture the commercial market.')
    • Key statistic: One impactful number (e.g., 'A $30 billion investment in EV and battery development by 2025.')"

By providing a "few-shot" example, you give the model a precise template to follow, resulting in a much more consistent and useful output.

docs.title: 2. Ask the AI to "Think Step-by-Step" 👣
docs.text:
For complex questions, especially those involving reasoning, data, or logic, you can get more accurate answers by asking the AI to show its work. Forcing it to slow down and explain its process often prevents it from making a quick, intuitive leap to the wrong conclusion.

  • Standard prompt: "Based on the attached sales data, what is our fastest-growing customer segment?"
  • A better prompt: "Based on the attached sales data, think step-by-step to determine our fastest-growing customer segment. First, identify all the customer segments. Second, calculate the year-over-year growth rate for each. Finally, state which segment has the highest growth rate and what that rate is."

This "chain-of-thought" approach not only improves the accuracy of the answer but also makes the reasoning transparent, allowing you to easily verify its logic.

docs.title: 3. Give the AI Your Documents 📎
docs.text:
The most powerful way to provide context is to give the AI your actual source material. Instead of describing a document, chart, or data table, upload it directly. This grounds the AI's response in your specific reality, eliminating generic answers.

  • Instead of describing: "My company's latest report shows that sales in the Northeast region have declined while sales in the South have grown. Why might this be?"
  • Try uploading the file: "Here is our Q3 sales report (sales_report.pdf). Analyze the regional performance data on page 8 and provide three potential hypotheses for the sales decline in the Northeast."

This is the entire principle behind NotebookLM. By uploading your documents, you turn the AI into an expert on your content.

docs.title: 4. Choose the Right Tool for the Job: Speed vs. Power ⚡
docs.text:
Many AI systems offer different models, often a faster, lighter version (like "Flash") and a more powerful, advanced one (like "Pro"). It's helpful to know when to use each.

  • Use the Fast Model (Flash) for: Quick, simple tasks where speed is important. This includes summarizing a short email, brainstorming a quick list of ideas, or reformatting text. Think of it as a nimble sports car for everyday errands.
  • Use the Powerful Model (Pro) for: Complex, nuanced tasks that require deep reasoning. This includes analyzing a dense research paper, drafting a detailed strategic plan, or solving a multi-step problem. Think of this as a heavy-duty truck for a major project.

A good workflow: Start with the faster model. If the quality of the response isn't good enough or the task is very complex, switch to the more powerful model.

docs.title: Working with AI
docs.text:
Throughout this course, you will act as a theorist and business analyst, and just like a professional in the field, you will be empowered by cutting-edge tools to help you do your work more effectively. This lesson introduces you to two powerful AI tools—Gemini and NotebookLM—and teaches you how to use them to elevate the quality of your graded deliverables.

Our goal is not to have AI write your paper for you. Instead, we will treat AI as a research partner—a powerful assistant that can help you find, synthesize, and organize information so that you can focus on the most important part of the assignment: your own critical thinking and unique analysis.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
Upon completion of this lesson, you will be able to:

  • Understand the role of AI as a "thinking partner" for learning and analysis.
  • Differentiate between a general-purpose AI assistant (Gemini) and a source-grounded analysis tool (NotebookLM).
  • Construct effective prompts that provide clear context and instructions to AI tools.
  • Critically evaluate AI-generated responses for accuracy, bias, and completeness.
  • Apply best practices for using AI ethically and effectively to deepen your understanding without compromising academic integrity.
  • Use NotebookLM to conduct a source-based analysis of a company.
  • Use Gemini to brainstorm and extend your analysis with creative and strategic thinking.

docs.title: The Big Picture
docs.text:
Why Your Brain is an AI's Best Friend

To work effectively with AI assistants like Gemini, you first need to understand their fundamental design. At its core, a Large Language Model (LLM), The technology behind AI, is a next-token prediction engine.

Think of it like a massive game of "complete the sentence." If I say, "The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy...", your brain instantly predicts the next word is likely "dog." LLMs do the same thing, but on an unimaginable scale. They've been trained on a colossal amount of text from the internet, books, and articles. Based on this data, they calculate the most statistically probable next "token" (a word or piece of a word) to follow any given sequence of text.

This simple-sounding mechanism is incredibly powerful. It's what allows an AI to write an email, summarize a report, or even generate computer code. It is a master of linguistic patterns.

However, this design also has built-in limitations that you must understand. Because the AI is just predicting the most plausible sequence of words, it has no true understanding, no database of facts, and no inherent sense of truth. This can lead to common problems:

  • Hallucinations: The AI can generate confident-sounding, plausible, but completely false information because the false words were statistically likely to follow the preceding ones.
  • "Middle-of-the-Road" Responses: When asked a question, the AI often generates the most common, average, or widely held view from its training data. This can be bland, uninspired, and lack unique insight.
  • Bias Reinforcement: The model will reflect the biases present in its vast training data, sometimes reinforcing stereotypes or one-sided views without being explicitly asked to.

Your job as a critical thinker is to counteract these tendencies. You are the source of intent, truth-checking, and creativity. Here are four strategies to do just that.

docs.title: 1. Be the Pilot, Not the Passenger
docs.text:
The AI's tendency is to follow the most probable path. Your job is to give it a specific, high-quality flight plan to force it off the default route. Actively navigate the conversation with clear and detailed instructions.

  • Instead of this (Passenger): "Tell me about Ford's EV strategy." (This invites a generic, predictable summary).
  • Try this (Pilot): "Act as a skeptical automotive journalist. Write a three-paragraph analysis of Ford's Q2 2025 earnings call, focusing on how their stated EV production targets conflict with their reported supply chain vulnerabilities. End with a question for the CEO."

This detailed prompt gives the AI a role (journalist), a task (analysis), context (Use Ford's Q2 2025 earnings as the background information for this task), a constraint (focus on conflict), and a format (three paragraphs with a final question). You are steering it toward insightful output.

docs.title: 2. Be a Healthy Skeptic
docs.text:
Never take the AI's first answer at face value. More importantly, use the AI to challenge your own thinking. Its ability to instantly adopt a different persona is a powerful tool for spotting weaknesses in your own arguments.

  • Instead of this (Accepting): "Okay, that's a good summary of the risks."
  • Try this (Skeptical): "Now, act as Ford's Head of Investor Relations. Write a rebuttal to the risks you just outlined. Which of those points is the weakest or most speculative?"

This forces the AI to move beyond the probable first answer and explore the topic from multiple angles. It helps you, the human, develop a more robust and nuanced understanding.

docs.title: 3. Experiment and Refine Interactively
docs.text:
Think of your first prompt as a hypothesis. The AI's response is the first set of experimental data. Now, you must refine your experiment to get a better result. Treat the interaction as a dynamic conversation, not a one-shot query.

  • Initial Prompt: "Brainstorm some marketing slogans for a new Ford electric truck."
  • AI's Generic Response: "Ford: Powering the Future," "The Electric Workhorse," "Built Ford Tough, Built for Tomorrow."
  • Refining Prompt: "Those are too generic. Let's try again. The target audience is construction contractors in Texas who are skeptical of EVs. Give me five slogans that directly address their potential concerns about range, toughness, and charging infrastructure."

The second prompt provides crucial context and constraints, leading to a much more targeted and creative output.

docs.title: 4. Use AI as Your Personal Tutor 🎓
docs.text:
One of the most powerful uses of an LLM is to make complex information accessible. It can act as a tireless translator or tutor, helping you learn faster and more deeply. This transforms the AI from a tool you wonder about into a partner you learn with.

Let's say you're reading a dense financial document (like a 10-K report) and encounter a difficult concept.

  • Instead of just skipping it, ask the AI: "This report mentions 'unfunded pension liabilities.' Can you explain what that means in simple terms, using an analogy of a family budget? Why would an investor care about this number?"

This approach allows you to use the AI to build your foundational knowledge. You are not asking it for the answer to an assignment; you are asking it to help you understand the material so you can produce a better, more insightful assignment yourself. This is the key to using AI without sacrificing your own learning.

docs.title: Meet Your AI Assistants
docs.text:
The Brainstormer and The Researcher

Not all AI tools are the same. For this course, we will use two powerful but very different assistants. Knowing which one to use for which task is the key to working effectively. Think of them as two specialists on your team: the creative brainstormer and the meticulous researcher.

docs.title: Google Gemini
docs.text:
Your Creative and Reasoning Partner 🧠

Gemini is your brilliant, world-read collaborator. It has been trained on a vast and diverse dataset of text and code, making it an expert in language, logic, and reasoning. It's the perfect partner for expansive, creative, and exploratory thinking.

Imagine you're sitting down with an expert who has read most of the public internet. They can explain anything from quantum physics to Shakespearean literature, draft a marketing plan, or help you brainstorm ideas for a new product.

Strengths:

  • Brainstorming and Ideation: When you're facing a blank page, Gemini is your best friend. You can ask it to generate ideas, explore different angles, and act as a creative sounding board.
  • Explaining Complex Topics: It can take a complex idea—like a financial derivative or a piece of legislation—and explain it in simple terms or with an analogy.
  • Drafting and Summarizing (General): Gemini can create a first draft of an email, a memo, or an essay on a general topic. It can also summarize broad concepts based on its general knowledge.
  • Strategic Thinking: You can ask it to "act as a consultant" and propose strategies, analyze hypothetical scenarios, or identify potential market opportunities.

Key Limitation: It is NOT source-grounded. Gemini's knowledge is vast but general. It does not know what's in the specific PDF you're reading or the lecture notes on your desk (unless you paste the text directly into your prompt). Because of this, its responses are based on the patterns from its training data, making it susceptible to the hallucinations we discussed earlier. Always verify its factual claims.

docs.title: Google NotebookLM
docs.text:
Your Source-Grounded Research Assistant 📚

NotebookLM is your specialist researcher. It's designed to be an expert only on the specific documents you provide it. More than just a chatbot, it's a persistent workspace designed for projects that span days, weeks, and even months.

Imagine handing a stack of specific reports, articles, and transcripts to a brilliant research assistant and saying, "Read these, and only these. Now, answer my questions based solely on what you've read." That is NotebookLM. It creates a personalized AI model grounded in your documents.

Strengths:

  • Source-Grounded Answers: Its most important feature. NotebookLM will only answer questions based on the sources you upload. When it provides an answer, it also provides a citation that takes you to the exact passage in your source document, making verification instant.
  • Summarizing Dense Materials: You can upload a 100-page annual report and ask NotebookLM to provide a five-bullet-point summary of the key financial results.
  • Finding Connections Across Sources: It can synthesize information from multiple documents. You can ask, "What are the common themes mentioned in the earnings call transcript and the CEO's interview?".
  • Integrating Your Own Thinking: NotebookLM allows you to write your own notes or save key AI insights. These notes become part of the source material, turning the AI into a partner that learns from and builds upon your unique ideas.

Key Limitation: It knows NOTHING beyond your sources. NotebookLM's greatest strength is also its limitation. If you haven't uploaded a document about a topic, it can't answer questions about it. This makes it highly accurate and reliable, but also narrowly focused.

docs.title: When Should You Use Each?
docs.text:
Here's a simple guide to choosing the right tool for the job:

Use Gemini when you need to... Use NotebookLM when you need to... 🚀 Go broad and brainstorm new ideas. 🎯 Go deep into a specific set of documents. 🤔 Understand a general concept you're unfamiliar with. 🔎 Find a specific fact within your sources. ✍️ Draft a first version of a text from scratch. 📝 Summarize the dense materials you already have. 💡 Think creatively and explore hypothetical scenarios. 🔗 Synthesize information across multiple provided reports. 🗣️ Have a quick, exploratory conversation. 🏗️ Build a long-term project with sources and your own notes.

By understanding these distinct roles, you can leverage both the expansive creativity of Gemini and the focused, factual precision of NotebookLM.

docs.title: A Guide to Using AI Tools Responsibly in This Course
docs.text:
Our Philosophy on AI

Artificial intelligence tools like Gemini and NotebookLM are transforming the professional world, and learning to use them effectively, ethically, and responsibly is now a critical career skill. In this class, we will not ban these tools. Instead, we will learn to use them as what they are: incredibly powerful assistants that can augment our thinking, enhance our productivity, and deepen our learning.

This guide is designed to provide clear principles and examples for how to engage with these tools in a way that supports your learning and upholds the standards of academic integrity.

The Core Principle

Our entire policy can be summarized in one sentence:

Our Policy

The work you submit must be a genuine product of your own intellectual effort, analysis, and learning.

AI can be a powerful partner in the process, but the final analysis, the core arguments, and the written expression must be yours. You are the analyst, the theorist, and the author; AI is your tool.

docs.title: What is FAIR USE? (How to Use AI to Enhance Your Learning)
docs.text:
You are encouraged to use AI tools in the following ways to support your work on the assignments in this course. Think of these as using a calculator for complex math or a search engine to find source material.

  • As an On-Demand Tutor:

    • To Clarify Concepts: "Explain the 'agency problem' to me. Use an analogy related to a sports team and its owner to help me understand."
    • To Explore Different Perspectives: "What are the strongest arguments *for* shareholder primacy?"

  • As a Brainstorming Partner:

    • To Generate Ideas: "I'm interested in Nike. Help me brainstorm three different 'conceptual focus questions' that connect its marketing strategy to its corporate culture."
    • To Structure Your Thoughts: "I'm working on my Company Analysis paper. Help me create a simple outline for the 'Evidence from Functional Levers' section based on a thesis that Nike is a stakeholder-focused company."

  • As a Research Assistant (Primarily with NotebookLM):

    • To Summarize Sources for Triage: Upload a long document like a 10-K report and ask for a summary of a specific section to help you identify where to focus your own deep reading.
    • To Find Evidence Within Your Sources: Ask questions like, "Based on my sources, find all mentions of 'supply chain ethics' and provide quotes with citations."

  • As a Writing Coach:

    • To Improve Your Own Writing: Paste a paragraph you have already written and ask, "Can you help me make this paragraph clearer and more concise?" or "Can you check this text for grammatical errors?"

docs.title: What is UNACCEPTABLE USE? (Academic Misconduct)
docs.text:
Submitting work that is not the product of your own intellectual effort is a serious violation of academic integrity. The following actions are considered academic misconduct in this course:

  • Plagiarism by AI: Copying and pasting sentences, paragraphs, or entire sections of text generated by an AI model and presenting them as your own writing.
  • Misrepresentation of Research: Using an AI to summarize an article or report and then using that summary in your work as if you have read and understood the original source yourself. Your analysis must be based on your own engagement with the materials.
  • Outsourcing Core Analysis: Providing an AI tool with the prompt for an assignment and having it perform the central analytical task.
    • Example of Misconduct: "Write an essay arguing that Tesla's management ideology is shareholder primacy, using evidence from its financial decisions and HR policies."
  • Submitting AI-Generated Content as Your Own: Generating any core component of an assignment (e.g., your "Analytical Narrative" or sections of your "Executive Report") and submitting it with only minor edits.

A Simple Rule of Thumb: Before you submit your work, ask yourself: "Could I confidently and thoroughly explain and defend every single sentence in this submission to the professor if asked?" If the answer is "no," you have likely crossed the line from fair use to academic misconduct.

docs.title: A CRITICAL WARNING: YOU ARE RESPONSIBLE FOR YOUR WORK
docs.text:
AI models are powerful, but they are not infallible. They can and do make mistakes, misunderstand context, create biased content, and "hallucinate" (make up facts and sources that seem plausible but are not true).

You are the human analyst in charge. If you submit a paper containing a factual error, a false source, or a flawed argument that originated from an AI tool, you are fully responsible for that error. You must critically evaluate, edit, and fact-check all information you use, regardless of its source.

Citing Your Use: Transparency is key. At the end of any assignment where you used an AI tool for fair use purposes (like brainstorming or editing), please include a brief "Process Note" explaining how you used it.

  • Example Process Note: "I used Gemini to brainstorm initial ideas for my conceptual focus question. I also used it to check my final draft of the Theoretical Narrative for grammatical errors."

This course is an opportunity to develop cutting-edge skills. Let's approach these new tools with curiosity, integrity, and a commitment to producing our best, most authentic work.

docs.title: The Big Picture
docs.text:
The goal of this paper is not to write a report on what a company does, but to write a persuasive analytical essay that explains why a company behaves the way it does. Think of yourself as an analyst whose job is to look past the headlines and marketing to uncover the deep-seated principles that drive a company's strategic decisions.

Your entire paper will be built around a single, powerful argument about the company's core management ideology.

docs.title: Your Thesis
docs.text:
The heart of your paper is your thesis statement. You will argue that your company's actions are best explained by one of two competing ideologies:

  1. Shareholder Primacy: The belief that a company's primary, and perhaps only, duty is to maximize wealth for its owners (the shareholders).
  2. Stakeholder Primacy: The belief that a company must balance the needs of its shareholders with the needs of other critical groups, such as its employees, customers, suppliers, and the community.

How to Spot the Clues:

Actions that might signal Shareholder Primacy Actions that might signal Stakeholder Primacy Aggressive stock buyback programs and high dividend payouts. Reinvesting profits into employee training and benefits. Layoffs and cost-cutting during periods of high profitability. Public commitments to using ethically-sourced materials. Executive compensation tied almost exclusively to stock price. Strong investment in product safety and quality beyond regulations. Lobbying against environmental or labor regulations. Long-term partnerships with suppliers that prioritize stability over price. Prioritizing speed-to-market over product quality. Corporate philanthropy and significant community involvement.

Your first step is to do some preliminary research and form a working thesis. Be open to changing your mind! The best papers often come from an analyst who changes their initial hypothesis based on the evidence they uncover.

docs.title: The Research Process
docs.text:
Strong arguments are built on strong evidence. Your analysis will be far more convincing if you use credible, primary sources rather than just general news articles. Here is your research checklist:

  • The "Must-Have" - The 10-K Annual Report: This is a company's legally required report to the government and is a treasure trove of information. You can find it on the "Investor Relations" section of any public company's website. Pay close attention to these sections:
    • Business: What the company says it does.
    • Risk Factors: What the company fears might go wrong.
    • Management's Discussion & Analysis (MD&A): Where leadership explains the financial results. This is often where you find the "why" behind the numbers.
  • The Proxy Statement: This document details executive compensation and any shareholder proposals. It's the best place to find evidence of how leadership is incentivized.
  • Quarterly Earnings Call Transcripts: Listen to how the CEO and CFO talk to Wall Street analysts. What questions do they get asked? What language do they use? Do they talk more about "maximizing shareholder value" or "long-term investment in our people"?
  • Reputable Financial Journalism: Use sources like The Wall Street Journal, Bloomberg, The Financial Times, and The Economist for credible, in-depth analysis of your company.

docs.title: Structuring Your Analysis
docs.text:
Use the following structure to organize your paper. This is not a rigid template but a logical flow to help you build a persuasive case.

  1. Introduction: Start with a hook that introduces your company. By the end of the introduction, you must state your thesis clearly. For example: "While Johnson & Johnson publicly champions its commitment to customers and community, this paper will argue that its recent financial and operational decisions—from aggressive stock buybacks to its handling of litigation—demonstrate a firm adherence to a shareholder primacy model."
  2. The Company's Stated Strategy & Governance: Briefly discuss the company's official mission statement and its strategic goals. How does the company present itself? Does this official story align with your thesis, or is there a contradiction you plan to explore?
  3. Evidence from Functional Levers (The Body of Your Paper): This is where you present your evidence. For each function, use specific examples and explain how they support your thesis. Ask yourself probing questions:
    • Finance: Does the company use its cash to reward shareholders (buybacks, dividends) or to reinvest in long-term growth (R&D, employee development)? What does this choice tell you about its priorities? How is executive pay structured?
    • Marketing & Operations: Does the company compete on price (suggesting cost-cutting) or on quality and brand reputation? Are there public controversies related to its supply chain ethics or product safety? How does the company's relationship with its customers support your argument?
    • People & Talent: What is the company's reputation as an employer? Analyze its approach to layoffs, employee benefits, training programs, and diversity and inclusion. Are employees treated as an asset to be invested in (stakeholder view) or a cost to be managed (shareholder view)?
  4. Conclusion: Summarize your argument in a fresh and powerful way (don't just repeat the introduction). Briefly discuss the potential long-term consequences of the company's ideological stance. What are the risks or rewards of their chosen path?

docs.title: Writing Tips for A-Level Analysis
docs.text:
The difference between a B-grade paper and an A-grade paper is the depth of analysis. Your goal is to explain the "so what?" behind every piece of evidence.

Instead of This (Description) Try This (Analysis) "The company laid off 5,000 employees last year." "The decision to lay off 5,000 employees, despite the company posting record profits that same quarter, is compelling evidence of a shareholder-first ideology. The move prioritized immediate cost savings and a boost to the stock price over the well-being and stability of its workforce." "Apple spent $85 billion on stock buybacks." "Apple's decision to allocate a staggering $85 billion to stock buybacks—an amount that could have funded groundbreaking R&D or significantly increased employee wages—serves as powerful evidence for a shareholder-centric ideology where returning capital to investors takes precedence over other strategic priorities."

docs.title: Final Checklist
docs.text:
• Is my thesis stated clearly in the introduction?
  • Does every body paragraph help to support my thesis?
  • Have I used specific evidence from credible sources (like the 10-K)?
  • Have I drawn evidence from at least three different business functions?
  • Have I focused on analysis (the "why" and "so what") rather than just describing the company's actions?
  • Have I proofread the paper for clarity, grammar, and professional polish?

Good luck! I look forward to reading your analysis.

docs.title: The Big Picture
docs.text:
The goal of this assignment is not to write a report about a company; it is to build and explain your own integrated theory of management.

Think of yourself as a theorist. Your primary subject of analysis is the network of course concepts themselves—how they fit together, how they influence one another, and how they form a coherent system. You will create a Concept Map to visualize these relationships and a Theoretical Narrative to explain the logic and implications of your model.

A company of your choice will serve as your running "case study," providing concrete examples that bring your theoretical arguments to life. But remember, the star of this show is the network of ideas, not the company.

docs.title: The Heart of the Project
docs.text:
Every strong theory begins with a powerful question. The most important step in this assignment is to develop a conceptual focus question that will guide your thinking. This question must be about the relationship between ideas, not just facts about a company.

To understand the difference, study these examples:

Type of Question What it Asks Good for... Empirical Question (Avoid for this assignment) "What is Apple's strategy?" Your Final Company Analysis Project Conceptual Question (Pursue for this assignment) "How does the strategic concept of 'Competitive Advantage' depend on the effective integration of principles from Marketing (e.g., 'Brand Equity') and Operations (e.g., 'Supply Chain Efficiency')?" This Assignment

How to Develop a Strong Conceptual Question:

  1. Start with a Core Concept: Pick a major idea from the course that you find interesting (e.g., "Organizational Culture," "Shareholder Primacy," "Disruptive Innovation").
  2. Connect it to Other Concepts: Ask yourself, "What other ideas does this depend on? What does this idea influence?"
  3. Frame it as a "How" or "Why" Question:
    • "How does a firm's 'Management Ideology' create predictable tensions with the marketing goal of building long-term 'Brand Equity'?"
    • "In what ways do the principles of 'Organizational Culture' serve as the necessary foundation for executing a strategy of 'Disruptive Innovation'?"
    • "Why must an effective 'Operations Strategy' be directly informed by a company's financial model of 'Growth vs. Profitability'?"

Your question will be the central organizing principle for both your map and your narrative.

docs.title: The Visual Blueprint
docs.text:
The concept map is your visual thinking space. It is where you will organize the course concepts into a hierarchy and draw the cross-links that answer your focus question.

Step-by-Step Process:

  1. Place Your Focus Question at the Top: This orients you and your reader immediately.
  2. Identify Your "Tier 1" Concepts: These are the 2-4 major concepts that are central to your question. Arrange them prominently on the map.
  3. Build Out the Hierarchy ("Tier 2" and "Tier 3"): Under each main concept, add related sub-concepts. For example, under "Marketing Strategy," you might have "Brand Equity," "4 P's," and "Market Segmentation." This shows the hierarchical relationship.
  4. Draw and Label Cross-Links: This is the most critical step. Draw lines connecting concepts from different hierarchies. On each line, you must write a short phrase that explains the relationship. This is where your analysis becomes visible.
    • A line connecting "Supply Chain Efficiency" to "Brand Equity" might be labeled: "can undermine by sourcing low-quality materials."
    • A line connecting "Organizational Culture" to "Competitive Advantage" might be labeled: "creates a difficult-to-imitate source of."
  5. Add Illustrative Company Examples: Sparingly, add very brief examples from your chosen company to ground your conceptual points. A box coming off "Disruptive Innovation" might say: "e.g., Netflix's shift from DVDs to streaming." Keep these brief—they are illustrations, not the main point.

docs.title: Theoretical Narrative
docs.text:
Your narrative is a formal essay that answers your conceptual focus question. It should follow the logic of your map and explain your theoretical argument in detail.

Key Components of an "A-Level" Narrative:

  1. A Clear Introduction and Thesis: Start by stating your conceptual focus question. Your thesis statement should be a direct and concise answer to that question.
    • Example Thesis: "This essay argues that sustainable 'Competitive Advantage' is not just a strategic choice, but an emergent property that arises when a firm's 'Marketing Strategy' and its 'Operations Strategy' are in perfect alignment. When they are misaligned, one function will inevitably undermine the other, leading to strategic failure."
  2. Focus on Analyzing Concepts: The body of your paper should be organized around the conceptual claims you are making. Use your map as your outline. Each paragraph should explain a key connection you've identified.

  3. Use Your Company as Evidence, Not the Subject: This is the most important distinction. Your claims should be about the theories. Use the company to provide vivid, real-world proof of your theoretical points. Study this contrast:

    Instead of This (Subject is the Company) Try This (Subject is the Theory) "Tesla has a powerful brand. Its operations are also very innovative. This combination gives it a competitive advantage." "The concept of 'Brand Equity' is often viewed as a purely marketing function, but this view is incomplete. A brand's promise is only sustainable if the firm's 'Operational Capabilities' can consistently deliver on it. For instance, Tesla's brand promises cutting-edge innovation. This promise would be worthless if its operations were incapable of producing high-performance electric vehicles at scale. This illustrates how brand and operations are not separate pillars, but a tightly woven fabric." 4. A Strong Conclusion: Summarize the answer to your focus question. What are the broader implications of your theory? Why is it important for a manager to understand the connections you've outlined?

docs.title: Final Checklist
docs.text:
• Is my focus question clearly stated and conceptual in nature?
  • Does my concept map show both hierarchy and labeled cross-links?
  • Does my narrative have a clear thesis that answers my focus question?
  • Is the main subject of my narrative the relationship between concepts?
  • Do I use my company examples briefly and effectively to illustrate my theoretical points?
  • Have I proofread both the map and the narrative for clarity and professionalism?

This assignment is designed to be challenging and rewarding. It will equip you with a powerful mental model of management that will serve you well in the final project and beyond. I look forward to seeing your theories take shape!

docs.title: Course Description
docs.text:
Course Description and Learning Objectives

Business organizations touch our lives in a variety of ways: we use their products and services, we accept them as our employers, we invest our money in them, and we let them shape our communities. Whether you become a doctor, an artist, an engineer, or an entrepreneur, your life will be intertwined with the world of business. Making critical life decisions—choosing a job, making a financial investment, or even understanding the news—can be enhanced by a fundamental understanding of how businesses work. Helping you build this durable intellectual framework is the primary objective of this course.

Our journey this semester is built around a central question: How do organizations transform ideas, people, and capital into value in a complex and ever-changing world? We will tackle this question in three parts:

  1. The Playing Field: We begin by exploring the external world in which all businesses operate. We will discuss the role of product and factor markets, the power of governing ideologies like shareholder and stakeholder primacy, and the critical influence of leadership and corporate governance. This sets the stage—the opportunities and constraints that every organization faces.

  2. The Game Plan & The Engine: Next, we dive into the heart of management by focusing on Strategy. We’ll ask how leaders make crucial choices to create a sustainable competitive advantage. Then, with strategy as our guide, we will open up the “black box” of the firm to see how it functions as an Organizational Engine. We will investigate the fundamental tension every company faces: how to design an efficient machine for executing today's strategy while also cultivating an adaptive organism capable of innovating for tomorrow.

  3. The Functional Levers & Applied Analysis: Finally, we will examine the essential business functions—Finance, Marketing, Operations, People & Talent, and Technology Management—not as isolated silos, but as the interconnected levers managers pull to bring their strategy to life. Throughout the semester, you will apply these concepts in an experiential learning project, acting as an analyst to decode the strategy and performance of a major corporation.

By the end of this course, you should be able to:

  • Enumerate, describe, and analyze major business function decisions.
  • Analyze and explain the strategic management decisions of a company and their potential outcomes.
  • Understand, evaluate, and apply foundational concepts that underlie contemporary management ideology.
  • Pursue more specialized courses on business and management.

docs.title: Attendance & Participation Policy
docs.text:
1. Policy Rationale

Success in this course requires consistent engagement and active participation. This course is designed as a hands-on, collaborative workshop. In-class sessions are not lectures but opportunities to collaborate, troubleshoot, and learn from your peers. Your presence is therefore critical not only for your own learning but also for the learning of your project team and the class as a whole. This policy is intended to reflect the professional standard of accountability expected in the workplace.

2. Attendance Requirement

A minimum attendance rate of 80% is required to pass this course. Failure to meet this requirement will result in the final course grade being lowered by one full letter grade (e.g., from a B+ to a C+).

3. Definition of an Absence

Any instance of missing a scheduled class for any reason will be recorded as an absence. However, a distinction is made for documented, extenuating circumstances.

  • Extenuating Circumstances (Excused): These are serious, unavoidable events that prevent attendance and will not count toward the 80% threshold. They are limited to:

    • Documented medical emergencies or significant illness.
    • A death in the immediate family.
    • University-sanctioned activities (e.g., athletic competitions, academic conferences) with prior official notification.
    • Recognized religious observances.

  • Non-Extenuating Circumstances (Unexcused): These absences, even when communicated in advance, will be counted as an absence and apply toward the 80% threshold. Examples include, but are not limited to:

    • Job interviews or work-related commitments.
    • Personal travel or family vacations.
    • Appointments that could be scheduled outside of class time.
    • Minor illnesses without medical documentation.

4. Notification Procedure

  • For any absence, students are expected to notify the instructor via email prior to the start of class as a matter of professional courtesy.
  • To have an absence classified as an "Extenuating Circumstance," official documentation (e.g., a note from a medical professional, a university notice) must be provided to the instructor within one week of the absence.

5. Tardiness

Arriving more than 10 minutes late or leaving more than 10 minutes before the class concludes is disruptive to the learning environment. Every three instances of tardiness or early departure will be recorded as one unexcused absence.

The theories and frameworks we discuss in class can sometimes feel abstract. The purpose of these weekly video assignments is to bridge the gap between theory and practice. The goal of these short assignments is to help you:

  • Develop your analytical eye to spot business concepts "in the wild."
  • Deepen your understanding of the course material by applying it to current events and leadership perspectives.
  • Build a mental library of real-world examples that you can use in class discussions and for your final company analysis project.
  • Practice communicating complex ideas clearly and concisely.

  3. Write a Brief Commentary: Your task is to explain the connection you found. This is not a summary of the entire video. Instead, it is a focused analysis of how a specific moment in the video relates to a specific concept from our course.

docs.title: Submission Guidelines & Format
docs.text:
To ensure these assignments are focused and manageable, please adhere to the following structure and length.

  • Submission Format: A single text entry or document upload.
  • Length: 250-350 words. This is a firm range. The goal is focused, high-quality analysis, not a long essay.

  • Structure: Please structure your submission with the following three headings:

    1. Course Concept: Name the single concept you have chosen to focus on.
    2. Video & Timestamp: Name the video and provide the specific timestamp (e.g., from 12:15 to 13:00) of the moment you are analyzing.
    3. Commentary: Write your analysis. In this section, you should:
      • Briefly define the course concept in your own words.
      • Describe what is happening at your chosen moment in the video (e.g., "The CEO argues that...").
      • Clearly explain the connection. How does this moment serve as a practical example or a counterpoint to the academic concept?

docs.title: Example Submission
docs.text:
Here is a sample submission to guide you. (This is a hypothetical example based on our course content).

Course Concept: Stakeholder Primacy

Video & Timestamp: "CEO of Patagonia on Corporate Responsibility," at 5:22

Commentary: Stakeholder primacy is the management ideology that a corporation should be run for the benefit of all its stakeholders—including employees, customers, suppliers, and the community—not just shareholders. This contrasts with shareholder primacy, which focuses exclusively on maximizing shareholder wealth.

At the 5:22 mark of the interview, the CEO of Patagonia discusses the company's decision to invest heavily in a new, more expensive supply chain that guarantees fair wages for workers and uses environmentally sustainable materials. He states, "Our profitability is important, but it's only one measure of our health. If our supply chain is harming the planet or treating people unfairly, then we aren't a successful company, even if the stock price is high."

This statement is a perfect real-world application of stakeholder primacy. The CEO is explicitly articulating a trade-off between maximizing short-term profit (by using a cheaper supply chain) and fulfilling the company's obligations to its other stakeholders (employees, the community, and the environment). His definition of a "successful company" is not limited to financial returns, but encompasses a broader set of ethical and social responsibilities, which is the core tenet of stakeholder theory.

docs.title: Concept Map & Analytical Narrative
docs.text:
The Purpose: The goal of this assignment is to build your own integrated theory of management. You will create a Concept Map to visually structure the relationships between the course's core ideas and a Theoretical Narrative to explain the logic and implications of those connections.

Your primary subject of analysis is the network of course concepts themselves—their hierarchy, their dependencies, and the way they link together to form a coherent system. Your chosen company will serve as a consistent "case study" throughout your narrative, providing concrete examples that illustrate your theoretical points in action.

This assignment focuses on the "why" and "how" of the theories, while the final Company Analysis project will focus on the "what" and "so what" of the company's empirical actions.

The Anchor: Your Conceptual Focus Question The heart of this assignment is a single, powerful conceptual focus question. Unlike the empirical question for your final project, this question should be about the relationship between theoretical ideas.

  • Empirical Question (for the Final Project): "How does Apple's culture of secrecy and product design excellence create a sustainable competitive advantage?" (This question is about Apple).
  • Conceptual Question (for This Assignment): "How does the strategic concept of 'Competitive Advantage' depend on the effective integration of principles from Marketing (e.g., 'Brand Equity') and Operations (e.g., 'Supply Chain Efficiency')?" (This question is about the theories, using a company like Apple for examples).

More Examples of Good Conceptual Focus Questions:

  • "How can a company's 'Management Ideology' (e.g., Shareholder Primacy) create predictable tensions with the marketing goal of building long-term 'Brand Equity'?"
  • "In what ways do the principles of 'Organizational Culture' and 'Team Composition' serve as the necessary foundation for executing a strategy of 'Disruptive Innovation'?"

Analysis vs. Description

To clarify how a theoretical analysis and a empirical description differ, consider this example:

Instead of This (Describing the Company) Try This (Analyzing the Concepts) "Patagonia has a strong organizational culture that values environmentalism. It uses this to build a loyal customer base, which is its brand equity." "This analysis argues that a stakeholder-centric 'Management Ideology' is a direct prerequisite for building authentic 'Brand Equity.' For a company like Patagonia, its stakeholder actions—such as environmental advocacy—are not separate from its marketing; they are the marketing. This illustrates how a firm's internal 'Organizational Culture' can be its most powerful and difficult-to-imitate marketing asset, creating a brand that purely profit-driven competitors cannot easily replicate."

The Final Deliverables:

  1. The Concept Map: A visual diagram showing the hierarchy and cross-linkages between a wide range of course concepts. Your map should be organized to help answer your focus question.
  2. The Theoretical Narrative (1,000 - 1,250 words): This is a formal essay that answers your conceptual focus question. This is not a report about your company. It is a theoretical argument where you use examples from your chosen company to illustrate your points about how different business concepts interact. Your primary claims should be about the theories themselves.

docs.title: Company Analysis
docs.text:
The Purpose: This capstone assignment is your opportunity to synthesize everything you have learned in the course. You will conduct a comprehensive analysis of your chosen company, moving beyond simple description to develop a persuasive, evidence-based argument about the firm's core strategic drivers.

The Anchor: Management Ideology as the Lens for Analysis The central task of this paper is to analyze your company through the lens of management ideology. Your paper must advance a clear thesis arguing whether your company operates primarily from a shareholder primacy or a stakeholder primacy perspective. Every piece of evidence and analysis in your paper should be used to support this central thesis.

The Task: Analysis, Not a Report Your goal is to write an analytical essay, not a book report. You should assume your reader is familiar with the basic facts of your company and the definitions of course concepts. Your grade will depend on the quality of your analysis—how well you use evidence from the company's actions to support your argument about its ideology.

Recommended Structure:

  1. Introduction: State your thesis clearly. Which ideology drives the company, and what are the key reasons you believe this to be true?
  2. Strategy & Governance: Briefly describe the company's stated strategy and governance structure. How do these initial elements align with your thesis?
  3. Evidence from Functional Levers: This is the core of your paper. Dedicate sections to analyzing the company's actions in its key business functions. For each function, provide specific evidence and explain how it supports your thesis about the company's ideology.
    • Finance: How do decisions about stock buybacks, dividends, capital investments, and executive compensation reveal the company's priorities?
    • Marketing & Operations: How do choices about product quality, supply chain ethics, pricing, and customer relationships support your argument?
    • People & Talent: How do HR policies regarding compensation, layoffs, training, and diversity and inclusion serve as evidence for your thesis?
  4. Conclusion: Summarize your argument. Briefly discuss the potential long-term implications of the company's chosen ideology.

docs.title: Teaching Approach
docs.text:
The primary objective of this course is to equip students with a practical and durable framework for analyzing business as an intergral part of our society, its challenges and opportunities.

My teaching methodology is centered on application. The course is structured as a hands-on workshop where learning is achieved by applying core business concepts to real-world situations. The focus is on developing analytical and problem-solving skills through project-based work, rather than on the memorization of abstract theories.

The curriculum is designed to demonstrate the interconnectedness of key business functions. Students will learn to analyze how decisions in areas like finance, marketing, and operations influence one another and impact overall strategy.

Upon completion, students are expected to be able to:

  • Analyze a company’s strategic decisions and performance using evidence-based reasoning.
  • Explain the relationships between the primary functions of a business.
  • Construct and defend a persuasive, data-driven business analysis.
  • Critically evaluate different management ideologies and their consequences.

Students are encouraged to use modern professional tools, including AI assistants, responsibly and ethically. The goal is to build proficiency with the technologies used in the contemporary workplace while emphasizing the importance of individual critical thinking and analytical ownership.
